parole.significato: forms diminutives from nouns and adjectives, or gives a particularizing sense
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -et. Doublet of -ito.
From French -pède, from Latin pedis.
Borrowed from French agir, itself borrowed from Latin agere.

parole.significato: German (of, from or relating to Germany)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French allemand, from Late Latin Alemannus, from Proto-Germanic *Alamann-, most likely from the roots of all + man.
Borrowed from French alternatif, from Latin alternātīvus.
Unadapted borrowing from French amateur. Doublet of amador.

Borrowed from French amphibole, from Latin amphibolus (“ambiguous”), from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβολος (amphíbolos, “put round, encompassing”), from ἀμφί (amphí, “around, on both sides”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”).
Borrowed from French envers, from Latin inversus. Doublet of inverso and envés.
Borrowed from French anis, from Latin anīsum, from Ancient Greek ἄνῑσον (ánīson).
Borrowed from French argentaffin, from Latin argentum (“silver”) and affinis. First coined by P. Masson in 1914.
Derived from French harmonium, from Latin harmonia.
From French autochtone, from Latin autochthŏnes, from Ancient Greek αὐτόχθων (autókhthōn), which comes from αὐτός (autós, “own”) + χθών (khthṓn, “land”).

parole.significato: to tell, tip off, notify, inform
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aviser, from Latin advisāre. Cognate with English advise.
Borrowed from French babouine, from Latin papione, singular ablative of papio, ultimately from Egyptian Baba or Babi, the baboon god.
Borrowed from French baie, from Late Latin baia, perhaps of Iberian origin.
Borrowed from French balance, from Late Latin *bilancia.
Borrowed from French banal, from Medieval Latin bannālis, from bannum.
Borrowed from French baie. Cognate with English bay (“bay leaf, bay laurel”).
Borrowed from French vermillon, ultimately from Latin vermiculus, diminutive of vermis (“worm”).
Borrowed from French bicyclette, from Latin bi- (“two”) + Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle, wheel”). By surface analysis, biciclo + -eta.

parole.significato: each of the metallic terminals of certain electrical machines and apparatus, intended for the connection of conductive…
parole.testo: From French borne, from Medieval Latin (Merovingian) bodina, butina (“limit, boundary”), a Celtic/Transalpine Gaulish borrowing, from Proto-Celtic *bonnicca (“boundary”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn (“bottom, base”), see also *bundos.

Borrowed from French bouteille, from Late Latin butticula, diminutive of buttis (“cask, barrel”). First attested in 1721, displaced frasco in general use. Doublet of botija. Cognate with English bottle.
Borrowed from French Breton.
Borrowed from French broche.
Borrowed from French boucle, from Latin buccula. Cognate with English buckle.

parole.significato: a virile man who engages in sexual intercourse with other men (often effeminate), where he is always the penetrator, an…
parole.testo: Cognate to bujarrón, from French bougeron (see French bougre), originally from Medieval Latin Bulgarus (“Bulgarian”), from Old Church Slavonic блъгаринъ (blŭgarinŭ, “Bulgarian”), used as an insult by the Crusaders, who considered the Bulgarians heretics because of their membership in the Orthodox Ch
Borrowed from French bouquet, from Old French bochet, from bois, from Early Medieval Latin boscus (“grove”), borrowed from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz.
Learned borrowing from French bolide, from Latin bolis, from Ancient Greek βολίς (bolís).

Borrowed from French calife, from Medieval Latin calipha, from Arabic خَلِيفَة (ḵalīfa, “vicar, successor”). Displaced patrimonial instance halifa as borrowed directly from Andalusian Arabic خَلِيْفَة (ẖalífah).
Borrowed from French capot. Doublet of capó.
Borrowed from French capot. Doublet of capote.

Borrowed from French carabine (“carbine”), from Old French carabin (“mounted rifleman”), perhaps from escarrabin (“corpse bearer during the plague”, literally “carrion beetle”), from scarabée (“dung beetle”), from Latin scarabaeus (“beetle”), from Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, “beetle”).
Borrowed from French carbone, coined by Lavoisier, from Latin carbōnem, whence also the inherited doublet carbón (“coal, charcoal”).
Borrowed from French échalote, from Middle French eschalote, from Old French eschaloigne, from Latin ascalonia (cēpa) (literally “onion of Ascalon”). Doublet of escalonia.
Borrowed from French champignon.
Borrowed from French champagne, from Champagne, from Late Latin campania. Doublet of campaña.
Borrowed from French chamois, from Late Latin camōx. Doublet of gamuza.
Borrowed from French chancre, from Latin cancer. Doublet of cáncer and cancro.
Borrowed from French chapeau, from Early Medieval Latin cappellus. Doublet of chapó (also from French), capelo (from Italian), and capillo (inherited).

parole.significato: used to express appreciation; hat tip
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chapeau, from Early Medieval Latin cappellus. Doublet of the inherited capillo, and of capelo (from Italian), as well as chapeo, also from the French word.
Unadapted borrowing from French chef. Doublet of jefe and cabo.
From agua de Colonia, from French eau de Cologne, ultimately from Latin Colōnia Claudia Āra Agrippīnēnsium, Cologne, the current city in Germany, and cognate of English colony.
From French compost (“mixture of leaves, manure, etc., for fertilizing land" also "condiment”), from Latin compositus (“composed”).
Borrowed from French commune.

parole.significato: control, or running of a business
parole.testo: Borrowed from French contrôle.
Borrowed from French cornaline. Doublet of cornelina.

Borrowed from French crétin (“fool”), from Alpine French crestin (“Christian”), from Latin Christianus, from Ancient Greek Χριστιανός (Khristianós, “Christian”), from Χριστός (Khristós, “Christ”) (+ -ιανός (-ianós, “-ian”)), from χριστός (khristós, “anointed”), from χρίειν (khríein, “to anoint; to r

parole.significato: croissant (a flaky roll or pastry in a form of a crescent)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French croissant. Doublet of creciente.
Borrowed from French centime.
Borrowed from French dame, from Latin domina. Doublet of dueña.

Borrowed from French déroute (“rout”), from Old French desroter (“to disband, to disperse”), from rote, route (“band, company, troop, group of armed men”), originally a substantivized feminine of rout (literally “broken”), from Latin ruptus, perfect passive participle of rumpō (“to break”). Borrowed from French déserter, from Late Latin desertare, from Latin desertus.
Borrowed from French diatribe.

Borrowed from French druide, assumed singular of attested plural Latin Druidae, from Gaulish [Term?] (compare Irish draoi (“druid, wizard”), Scottish Gaelic druidh (“charmer, sorcerer”)). More at English druid.
Borrowed from French ecthyma, from New Latin ecthyma, from Greek έκθυμα (ékthyma, “pustule”). First attested in 1832.
Borrowed from French éditer.
Borrowed from French entrevoir, from Vulgar Latin *intervidēre.
Borrowed from French scorbut, from Late Latin scorbutus.
Borrowed from French spondylose, from Latin spondy̆lus (“vertebra”). Equivalent to espondilo- + -osis.
Borrowed from French store.

Borrowed from French estragon (“tarragon”), from Middle French targon, from Medieval Latin tragonia, from Arabic طَرْخُون (ṭarḵūn), ultimately from Ancient Greek δρακόντιον (drakóntion, “dragonwort, Dracunculus vulgaris”), from δράκων (drákōn, “dragon”). Doublet of drago.
Borrowed from French évolution, Latin ēvolūtiōnem (“unrolling of a book”), from ēvolvō (“to unfold, unroll, clear up”). Cognate with Catalan evolució.
Borrowed from French explosif, ultimately from Latin explōsus, remodelled with the cognate suffix -ivo.

parole.significato: bassoon (musical instrument in the woodwind family)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fagot (“bundle of sticks”), referring to the wood used to make the instrument.
Borrowed from French faisan, from Latin phāsiānus, from Ancient Greek φασιανός (phasianós), from Φᾶσις (Phâsis).

Borrowed from French filet, from Middle French filet, from Old French filet (“strip, thread, ligament or filament”), from fil (with the diminutive suffix -et), from Latin fīlum (“string or thread”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰis-lom, from the root *gʷʰi-.

parole.significato: a size of type between breviario and lectura chica, standardized as 10 point
parole.testo: Borrowed from French philosophie.

Borrowed from French flan, from Old French flaon, from Late Latin fladō (“flat cake”), from Frankish *flaþō (“flat cake”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂t- (“broad, flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂- (“to spread out, be broad, be flat”).

parole.significato: flush (hand consisting of all cards with the same suit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French flux. Doublet of flujo and flojo.
Borrowed from French forge, from Latin fabrica. Doublet of fábrica, froga, and fragua.
Borrowed from French fraterniser, from Latin frāternus + French -iser.
Borrowed from French fraise (“strawberry”).
Probably borrowed from French fumer, from Latin fūmāre. Doublet of humar (which was inherited).

parole.significato: van (a covered vehicle used for carrying goods or people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fourgon.

Borrowed from French gaillard (“strapping, lively, strong”), from Old French gaillart (“spirited”), from Vulgar Latin *galia (“strength”), from Transalpine Gaulish *gal- (“strength”). Compare English Gaylord.
Borrowed from French galon, from Late Latin galum, galus (“measure of wine”), from Vulgar Latin *galla (“vessel”), possibly from Gaulish [Term?], ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“goblet”).
Borrowed from French génie, of Latin influence but based on Arabic جِنّ (jinn).
Borrowed from French gratuité, from Medieval Latin gratuitatis.
Borrowed from French hémicycle, from Latin hemicyclĭum, from Ancient Greek ἡμῐκῠ́κλῐον (hēmĭkŭ́klĭon). By surface analysis, hemi- + ciclo.
Borrowed from French hôtel. Doublet of hospital and hostal.
Borrowed from French immarcescible, a learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin immarcēscibilis.

Borrowed from French installer, from Middle French [Term?], from Medieval Latin īnstallāre (“to install, put in place, establish”), from Latin in- + stallum (“stall”), from Frankish *stall (“stall, position, place”), from Proto-Germanic *stallaz (“place, position”), from Proto-Indo-European *stelǝ-,

Borrowed from French javeline, from Old French javelline, diminutive of javelot (“spear”), from Vulgar Latin *gabalottus, from Gaulish *gabalos (compare Old Irish gabul (“fork”), Welsh gafl), from Proto-Celtic *gabalos (“fork, forked branch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰabʰlos (“fork, branch of tre

Borrowed from French lévrier, from Old French levrer, from Late Latin canem leporārium (literally “hare dog, harehound”), from Latin lepus (“hare”). By surface analysis, liebre + -el. Doublet of lebrero (“harehound”).
Borrowed from French litre, from Medieval Latin litra, from Ancient Greek λίτρα (lítra, “a Sicilian coin, a measure of weight”). Doublet of arrelde.
Borrowed from French longe, feminine form of lonc (“long”), from Latin longus. Doublet of luenga.
Borrowed from French lunel, a heraldic term based on lune (“moon”), from Latin lūna. Compare Italian lunello.
Borrowed from French macle, from Medieval Latin mascula, from a Germanic source.

Borrowed from French malle (“large suitcase; trunk”), from Middle French malle, from Old French male (“leather bag, leather or wooden travel-case”), from Frankish *malha (“leather bag”), from Proto-Germanic *malhō (“leather bag”), from Proto-Indo-European *molko- (“leather bag”).
Borrowed from French machine. Doublet of máquina.
Borrowed from French maçon (“mason”).
Borrowed from French menton, from Vulgar Latin *mentonem, from Latin mentum (“the chin, beard”).

parole.significato: menu (list of foods to be served at a meal)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French menu (“detailed list, menu”), noun use of menu (“small, detailed”), from Latin minūtus (“very small”). Doublet of menudo and minuto.

parole.significato: micelle (a colloidal aggregate, in a simple geometric form, of a specific number of amphipathic molecules which forms a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French micelle, from New Latin micella.

parole.significato: mine (excavation from which ore is taken)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mine.
Borrowed from French mode. Doublet of modo.
Borrowed from French munir.

parole.significato: washbag, (UK) toilet bag, toiletry bag, toiletry kit, (US) Dopp kit, sponge bag, ditty bag
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nécessaire (“necessary”), from Latin necessārius. Doublet of necesario. Compare English necessaire, Italian necessario and Portuguese nécessaire, German Necessaire.
Borrowed from French numismatique, based on Latin numismatem (“coin”), alternative form of nomisma, from Ancient Greek νόμισμα (nómisma, “coin, money”).
Borrowed from French oublée, from Ecclesiastical Latin oblāta, from oblāta hostia (literally “offered host”).
Borrowed from French ogive, from Latin augere.

parole.significato: Small ivory horn of knights from the Middle Ages; an olifant
parole.testo: Borrowed from French olifant.
Borrowed from French optimisme, from Latin optimus, equivalent to óptimo + -ismo.
Borrowed from French optimiste, from Latin optimus, equivalent to óptimo + -ista.
Borrowed from French ordinateur, from Latin ordinātor. By surface analysis, ordenar + -dor.
Borrowed from French orfèvre, based on or (“gold”) and Latin faber (“artisan, forger, smith”).
Borrowed from French organiser, from Medieval Latin organizāre, from Latin organum (“organ”).

Borrowed from French orgie, which explains the accentuation on -í-, from Latin orgia, from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia). According to Coromines and Pascual, first attested circa 1830, aside from an odd occurrence in Juan Boscán Almogáver (16th c.). The variant órgia is attested in writers aware of th
Borrowed from French parcelle, from Late Latin particella, diminutive of Latin particula.
Borrowed from French parc. First attested in 1607.
Borrowed from French patriote, from Late Latin patriōta, from Ancient Greek πατριώτης (patriṓtēs, “fellow countryman”).
Borrowed from French pays, from Old French païs, from Medieval Latin pagēnsis, from Latin pāgus (“country”). Compare Sicilian pajisi, Italian paese.

parole.significato: perceptive (having perception: insight, understanding or intuition)
parole.testo: Formed from Latin perceptus + -ivo, based on French perceptif, or borrowed from Medieval Latin perceptivus.
Borrowed from French pessimisme, from Latin pessimus, equivalent to pésimo + -ismo.
Borrowed from French pessimiste, from Latin pessimus, equivalent to pésimo + -ista.
Borrowed from French péjoratif, from Late Latin pejōrātus, perfect passive participle of pejōrō (“to make worse”), from pejor (“worse”).

parole.significato: iron (metal tool used for transferring heat)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French planche.
Borrowed from French place. Doublet of plaza.
Borrowed from French pleurésie, from Late Latin pleurīsis.
Borrowed from French plumier, from plume + -ier, ultimately from Latin plūma (“down, feather”).
Borrowed from French propulsif, from Latin prōpulsus.

parole.significato: prototype (an original object which is a basis for others)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prototype, a borrowing from Late Latin prōtotypos (“elemental form”), from Ancient Greek πρωτότυπος (prōtótupos, “first example”).

Borrowed from French prodrome, from New Latin prodromus (“precursor”), from Ancient Greek πρόδρομος (pródromos), from προ- (pro-, “before”) + δρόμος (drómos, “race”). By surface analysis, pro- + -dromo.
Borrowed from French poêle, from Latin patella. Doublet of padilla, paella, and paila.
Borrowed from French pupitre. Doublet of púlpito.
Borrowed from French péplum, from Latin peplum, from Ancient Greek πέπλων (péplōn), neuter of πέπλος (péplos). Doublet of peplum.
Borrowed from French radio-.
Borrowed from French ragoût.
Borrowed from French restaurant.
Borrowed from French restaurant.
Borrowed from French roulette, from the verb rouler, from Vulgar Latin *rotulare.
Borrowed from French route, from the Latin phrase via rupta (“a paved, cleared or 'broken' road”).
Borrowed from French sérigraphie, reduced from séricigraphie, based on Latin sēricum (“silk”).
Borrowed from French soporifique, from Latin sopor (“deep sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swepōr, from *swep-.
Unadapted borrowing from French souvenir.
From the noun terraplén (“embankment”), from French terre plein, from Latin terra + plānus.
Borrowed from French train.

parole.significato: crew of a ship, plane, or other craft
parole.testo: Modified from French interpolation, from Latin interpolātiōnem. Compare English interpolation.
Borrowed from French turbine, itself borrowed from Latin turbinem (“circular movement, top, reel, spindle”). Compare turbión, an inherited doublet through a Vulgar Latin variant. Cf. also torbellino.

Borrowed from French tartare, from Middle French Tartar, from Old French Tartar, from Medieval Latin Tartarus, from Old Turkic [script needed] (Tatar). Influenced by Latin Tartarus (“Hell (in Greek mythology)”), which is from Ancient Greek Τάρταρος (Tártaros).
Borrowed from French huissier, from Late Latin ostiarius.
Borrowed from French visa, from Latin visa, inflected form of vīsus (“seen; having been seen”), from Proto-Italic *wissos, from Proto-Indo-European *widtós, from *weyd- + *-tós.
Borrowed from French viser (“to aim”), ultimately from Latin visō (“to look at”).
Via French volée, from Latin volāre, equivalent to vuelo + -ear. Doublet of volar.
Borrowed from French élite.
Borrowed from French (voiture) omnibus, from Latin omnibus (“[for] all, everyone”).
